**Distortion** changes the *shape* of a wave by squashing its loudest parts. A changed shape means a
changed recipe of harmonics ([Sound 1](sound-harmonics.qmd)), so distortion *adds* harmonics that
weren't there. A little gives warmth; a lot gives the roar of a rock guitar.

**How to use the page.** Every effect on these pages has a **Source** menu (what goes in), a **Mix**
(how much of the effect you hear), and **Bypass** to switch it out and back in. The square graph is
the distortion **curve**: the input level runs across, the output level up. The dashed diagonal is
"no change".

## A sine wave in, harmonics out

<div class="sk" data-w="distortion" data-source="tone"></div>

The source starts as a pure **sine tone**: one spike on the spectrum. Raise **Drive** slowly.

- The curve bends over at the ends: loud parts of the wave can't get any louder.
- The scope shows the sine's peaks being flattened toward a square.
- New spikes appear on the spectrum at 3, 5, 7… times the frequency: **odd harmonics**, because the top
  and bottom of the wave are squashed the same way. That's the square-wave recipe.

Now try the other curves:

| Curve | What it does | Sound |
|---|---|---|
| **Soft clip** | bends over gradually | overdrive: a warm, singing tone, like a valve amp turned up |
| **Hard clip** | flat-tops the wave at a fixed level | fuzz: buzzy and aggressive |
| **Uneven (tube-like)** | squashes the top and bottom differently | adds **even** harmonics (2, 4, 6) too, which sound sweeter and fuller |
| **Wavefolder** | folds the peaks back down instead of flattening them | the West-coast synth sound: glassy, metallic, changes wildly with drive |
| **Bit crusher** | rounds the wave to a few steps | the gritty sound of old computers and samplers |

**Tone** is a low-pass after the distortion: almost every guitar amp has one, to tame the fizz that
heavy distortion adds at the top.

## Overdrive, distortion or fuzz?

Guitarists use three words, and the pedals really are different. All three clip the wave; they
differ in **how hard** they clip, **what shape** the clipping is, and what they do to the sound
**before and after**.

<div class="sk" data-w="distortion" data-source="riff" data-preset="Overdrive" data-title="Three pedals"></div>

Play the synth riff and step through the presets, with **Bypass** to compare with the clean sound.
Watch the curve and the scope.

| | Overdrive | Distortion | Fuzz |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Curve** | soft clip: bends over gently | hard clip: flat tops | lopsided: one side clips much sooner, and a dead zone in the middle |
| **Drive** | low: clean when you play softly, gritty when you dig in | high: distorted however softly you play | extreme: nearly a square wave |
| **Before** | cuts the bass so the low notes don't turn to mud (the "mid hump" of a Tube Screamer) | some bass cut | nothing: the full, fat low end goes in |
| **After** | a tone control | a darker tone control to tame the fizz | dark and woolly |
| **Sound** | a turned-up valve amp: warm, still sounds like the instrument | tight and aggressive: metal and hard rock | buzzy, spitting, raw: "Satisfaction", Hendrix, the White Stripes |
| **Inside** | diodes in the op-amp's feedback loop | diodes after the op-amp | two transistors pushed far past their limits |

Two things to try:

- On **Overdrive**, choose the **Uneven riff** source (loud and soft notes). The soft notes stay
  almost clean and the loud ones break up: overdrive responds to how hard you play. On **Distortion**
  every note is equally squashed.
- On **Fuzz**, play a **Sine tone** and lower the **Drive**. The tone starts to **sputter**: quiet
  parts of the wave fall into the dead zone and vanish. Fuzz pedals with an old, dying battery do this
  on purpose, and the note cuts out raggedly as it fades.

## On music

Switch the **Source** to *Chords* or the *Synth riff*. Distorting a chord sounds much messier than
distorting one note: every note's harmonics clash with the others', and the curve also creates new
frequencies at the *differences* between the notes (**intermodulation**). That's why heavy rock guitar
plays **power chords** (root and fifth only). The difference frequencies of a fifth are another
octave of the root, so it stays clean.

Try your own voice or instrument through it with **Microphone** (and headphones).
